opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's an interesting question, and I want to be careful here because a lot of what circulates is anecdotal.

The kind of evidence people usually point to is behavioral. You ask the model who it is, and occasionally it identifies itself as Claude or as ChatGPT. Or you notice stylistic fingerprints: certain phrasings, refusal templates, the way it structures a list or hedges an answer, that look very close to another lab's model. On its own I'd treat that as weak evidence. The open web is now saturated with outputs from ChatGPT and Claude: forum posts, scraped conversations, synthetic datasets people upload to Hugging Face. So any model pretrained on a recent crawl will absorb some of that, including the self-identification. A model saying "I'm Claude" doesn't mean someone deliberately ran a distillation pipeline against the Claude API.

Stronger evidence would be things that are hard to explain by contamination alone. For example, very high agreement on idiosyncratic outputs, or matching specific errors, quirks or jailbreak behaviors that wouldn't appear in public text. People in the security and watermarking community have been working on exactly this kind of model fingerprinting, and I think it's the right direction. But I haven't seen anything that I'd call conclusive for any particular model.

There's also a fairly mundane point: almost everyone uses frontier model outputs somewhere in post-training now. Synthetic data for SFT, LLM-as-judge for preference data, reward modeling. So "distilled from other models" exists on a spectrum, from wholesale imitation of another model's outputs to using a stronger model as one ingredient in the data pipeline. The labs' terms of service draw lines on that spectrum, but technically it's blurry.

From my angle, working on safety and adversarial robustness, the more interesting question is what gets inherited. If you distill from a model, do you also inherit its safety behavior, or just the surface form of refusals without the underlying robustness? My intuition is that you often get the latter. The model learns to sound like it refuses in the same way, but the boundary is shallower, so attacks that fail on the teacher can transfer surprisingly well, or even work better, on the student. That's something you can actually measure, and I think it matters more for the field than the provenance debate itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd start by saying that I'm not a frontier lab, so I'm looking at the same public evidence everyone else is, and I think you have to be a bit careful about how much weight you put on any single signal.

The thing people usually point to is behavioral. You prompt the model, it claims to be a different model, it says it was made by a different company, or it reproduces a refusal style or formatting quirks that look very characteristic of a particular competitor. And I understand why that's suggestive. But I think the inference from "the model says it's Claude" or "the model says it's GPT" to "they distilled from that model" is weaker than it looks. The entire public internet is now full of ChatGPT transcripts, Claude transcripts, people pasting outputs into forums, Reddit, GitHub issues. If you train on a web crawl from the last few years, you are going to absorb a lot of that style and a lot of those self-identification statements for free, without ever calling anyone's API. So identity confusion is honestly the weakest piece of evidence. It's consistent with distillation, but it's also consistent with just training on data that's downstream of those models.

The stronger version of the argument is more statistical. If you look at distributions over phrasing, over which hedges a model uses, over how it structures a chain of thought, and you find that one model is unusually close to another in ways that aren't explained by shared pretraining data, that starts to look more like targeted synthetic data generation. And there's work on this, fingerprinting approaches, looking at how well you can classify which model produced a given text, and then checking whether a new model's outputs cluster suspiciously close to a specific source. That's more compelling, but it's still correlational. You don't get a signature that says "these tokens were sampled from this API."

And then there's the part people don't talk about enough, which is that distillation in the broad sense is just... how everyone trains now. Everybody is generating synthetic data with their strongest internal models, everybody is doing rejection sampling, everybody is doing RL with some kind of judge. The question isn't "did they distill" in the abstract, it's "whose model did the generating." And that's genuinely hard to tell from the outside, because a model that's been distilled from a strong teacher and then post-trained extensively can look quite different on the surface while still carrying a lot of the teacher's inductive biases underneath.

So my honest read is: the evidence makes it plausible that there's some lineage through outputs of other labs' models somewhere in the pipeline, but I wouldn't say it's established, and I'd push back on the confident version of the claim. What I'd want to see is a controlled comparison, same prompts, same decoding, compare against a baseline model that we know was trained without API access, and see whether the similarity is actually anomalous or whether it's just what any model trained on the 2024-2025 internet ends up looking like.

And I'll say one more thing, which is that even if it is true, I think the interesting question from a research perspective is less about the ethics or the terms-of-service angle, and more about what it tells us about how much of a frontier model's capability is actually transferable through outputs alone. If you can get a large fraction of the way there just from sampling a strong model, that has real implications for how defensible a capability lead is, and for how we think about things like safety-relevant behaviors propagating from one model to another. That's the part I find genuinely interesting, independent of the specific Kimi case.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: was Kimi trained on outputs from other models, and what would count as convincing evidence of that? If the evidence is simply that it sometimes identifies itself as another model, that’s fairly weak. You could get that from training data containing conversations with that model. Similar phrasing or similar benchmark performance wouldn’t establish distillation either.

More interesting would be a consistent pattern of shared, unusual errors across carefully controlled prompts. That could suggest a connection, but you’d still have to distinguish distillation from shared training data or other common influences.

So I’d treat distillation as a plausible hypothesis, not an established conclusion. And I’d be careful about what follows from it: using another model’s outputs during training doesn’t, by itself, tell you how much of the resulting capability came from those outputs.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d be careful about the word “evidence” here. What exactly are we observing? If a model identifies itself as another model, or produces similar phrases, that’s compatible with distillation, but it doesn’t establish it. You could also get that from overlapping training data, synthetic data collected from multiple sources, or fairly similar post-training procedures.

And distillation itself covers several different things. Training on another model’s outputs is different from trying to reproduce its probability distribution, and neither necessarily means that all of the resulting capabilities came from that teacher.

So I would treat it as a hypothesis. To make a stronger claim, I’d want something that distinguishes it from those alternative explanations—ideally information about the training pipeline, or systematic behavioral similarities that are difficult to explain through shared data. From the question alone, we don’t have enough to conclude that Kimi was distilled from a particular model.
